permits.generic: Ask your city or county (or local council) which permits apply and how much notice they need. Common ones: special event or temporary use, tent, amplified sound, street or sidewalk use, signs, temporary food, alcohol, and occupancy.

US.label: Small business guide: licenses and permits (US federal)

UK.label: Organising a voluntary event: a 'can do' guide (UK government)

AU.label: Business licence and information service (Australian government)

alcohol.generic: Your local or state licensing office decides whether you need a license to sell or serve alcohol, and how long it takes. Selling usually needs one; free serving may too.

insurance.generic: Ask your insurance agent whether your policy covers this event, guests and off-site locations, and about one-day event cover and liquor liability.

US.label: Small business guide: business insurance (US federal)

taxes.generic: Selling at a temporary location may mean collecting sales tax there. Ask your tax office, accountant or the market organizer.

US.label: Small business guide: pay taxes (US federal)

accessibility.generic: Plan step-free entry, clear routes, seating, an accessible restroom, readable signs and a microphone or captions for talks. Ask guests about access needs when they sign up.

US.label: ADA guide for businesses open to the public (US Department of Justice)

charity_receipts.generic: Only a qualified charity can give donors a tax receipt. Agree with the charity who collects the money, who sends receipts and how its name and logo may be used.

US.label: Charitable contributions: quid pro quo disclosures (IRS)

gaming.generic: Raffles, auctions with chance elements and other games of chance are often restricted to registered charities and may need a permit. Check your state or local rules before selling tickets.

US.label: Tax-exempt organizations and gaming (IRS Publication 3079, PDF)

emergency.generic: Know your exits and the nearest hospital, keep a first aid kit, and decide who calls emergency services and from where.
